title: Heʻe nalu (Hawaiian surfing)
summary: Heʻe nalu, meaning to slide on a wave, is the Hawaiian practice of wave riding, once considered the exclusive privilege and pastime of aliʻi. Its origin is undated. Crew of Cook’s third expedition described riders at Kealakekua Bay in 1779. By the 1880s it had nearly vanished in places.

uncertainty.note: Tradition with no sourced founding date; hawaii.surf says it likely predates the islands themselves. The record spans the first European description (1779) to reports that it had nearly vanished in places by the 1880s.

when.display: Undated origin; described 1779; waning by the 1880s

where.modern_name: Kealakekua Bay, Hawaiʻi Island, United States
where.historical_name: Hawaiian Islands, where Cook’s crew observed riders in 1779

importance.justification: An ancient Hawaiian sport tied to rank and later the ancestor of modern surfing.

reviewer_note: The id says 1500 but no opened source dates the practice; the span is the first European description to reported near-disappearance. Neither source is scholarly; hawaii.surf is a general site and Kamehameha Schools is an educational institution. The pin is Kealakekua Bay with a wide uncertainty for the islands.
